item.title: Configuring GNOME, Nautilus, and Power Management via CLI on Fedora
item.description:
On Fedora Linux with the GNOME desktop, hardware, interface, file manager, and power management settings are distributed across GSettings schemas, D-Bus interfaces, and systemd-logind. Rather than clicking through graphical menus, you can discover the exact schema paths, inspect valid key ranges, monitor live changes, and script reproducible workstation setups directly from the terminal.

Discovering Schemas, Keys, and Valid Values

Before modifying any setting, you can query GNOME's GSettings database to locate the right schema, read key documentation, check allowed data types or enum values, and watch changes in real time.

Step 1: Search for Relevant Schemas

List all available schemas and filter them by keyword:

gsettings list-schemas | grep -i "power"

Alternatively, search recursively across all schemas and current values simultaneously:

gsettings list-recursively | grep -i touchpad

Step 2: Inspect Keys and Current Values

Once you have a schema name, list its available keys or print every key alongside its active value:

# List only key names in a schema
gsettings list-keys org.gnome.desktop.peripherals.touchpad

# List all keys and their current values
gsettings list-recursively org.gnome.desktop.peripherals.touchpad

Step 3: Read Key Descriptions and Allowed Ranges

To avoid invalid value errors, inspect a key's built-in description and check the exact values or range it accepts (booleans, integers, or string enums):

# Read a key's description
gsettings describe org.gnome.desktop.peripherals.touchpad two-finger-scrolling-enabled

# Check valid values or range for a specific key
gsettings range org.gnome.desktop.peripherals.touchpad scroll-method

Step 4: Monitor Live Changes from the GUI

If you want to identify which key a toggle in the Fedora Settings app modifies, run gsettings monitor on a schema and click the option in the GUI:

gsettings monitor org.gnome.desktop.peripherals.touchpad

Common GSettings Schemas Reference

Feature GSettings Schema
Touchpad org.gnome.desktop.peripherals.touchpad
Mouse org.gnome.desktop.peripherals.mouse
Keyboard org.gnome.desktop.peripherals.keyboard
Interface / Fonts org.gnome.desktop.interface
Power Management org.gnome.settings-daemon.plugins.power
Privacy / Lock org.gnome.desktop.screensaver
Window Focus org.gnome.desktop.wm.preferences
File Manager org.gnome.nautilus.preferences

Touchpad and Mouse Configuration

On a laptop such as a Lenovo ThinkPad, configuring tap-to-click, two-finger scrolling, and natural scrolling across both the touchpad and external mice is handled under org.gnome.desktop.peripherals.

Touchpad Preferences

  • Schema: org.gnome.desktop.peripherals.touchpad
# Enable tap-to-click
gsettings set org.gnome.desktop.peripherals.touchpad tap-to-click true

# Enable Natural Scrolling (reverse scroll)
gsettings set org.gnome.desktop.peripherals.touchpad natural-scroll true

# Enable two-finger scrolling
gsettings set org.gnome.desktop.peripherals.touchpad two-finger-scrolling-enabled true

Mouse Preferences

  • Schema: org.gnome.desktop.peripherals.mouse
# Inspect all mouse keys and current values
gsettings list-recursively org.gnome.desktop.peripherals.mouse

# Enable natural scrolling for an external mouse
gsettings set org.gnome.desktop.peripherals.mouse natural-scroll true

Panel Indicators and Color Schemes

GNOME refers to the top bar as the Panel and the application dock as the Dash. System-wide appearance, clock details, and battery percentage indicators live under org.gnome.desktop.interface, while extensions such as Dash to Dock use org.gnome.shell.extensions.dash-to-dock.

Top Panel Clock and Battery Readouts

# Show the day of the week alongside date/time
gsettings set org.gnome.desktop.interface show-datetime-day-of-week true

# Show seconds in the clock
gsettings set org.gnome.desktop.interface clock-show-seconds true

# Show battery percentage
gsettings set org.gnome.desktop.interface show-battery-percentage true

Switching Between Dark and Light Themes

The color-scheme key under org.gnome.desktop.interface controls GNOME's system-wide dark and light appearance:

# Activate Dark Mode
gsettings set org.gnome.desktop.interface color-scheme 'prefer-dark'

# Revert to Light / Default Mode
gsettings set org.gnome.desktop.interface color-scheme 'default'

# Check the currently active theme mode
gsettings get org.gnome.desktop.interface color-scheme

You can also toggle between both modes automatically in a script or alias:

CURRENT=$(gsettings get org.gnome.desktop.interface color-scheme)
if [ "$CURRENT" = "'prefer-dark'" ]; then
    gsettings set org.gnome.desktop.interface color-scheme 'default'
else
    gsettings set org.gnome.desktop.interface color-scheme 'prefer-dark'
fi

Configuring Nautilus Sorting and Folders First

Nautilus schema keys have evolved across recent GNOME and GTK releases. Folder-first sorting is managed upstream at the GTK FileChooser level rather than as a standalone folders-first key inside Nautilus.

Inspecting Nautilus and GTK FileChooser Keys

# Inspect Nautilus preference keys and valid sort orders
gsettings list-recursively org.gnome.nautilus.preferences
gsettings range org.gnome.nautilus.preferences default-sort-order

# Locate all directory-sorting keys across schemas
gsettings list-recursively | grep -iE "sort|folder"

Setting Sort Order and Enforcing Folders First

Configure Nautilus to sort by file type in ascending order, and enable sort-directories-first across both GTK 3 and GTK 4 schemas:

# Sort files by type in ascending order
gsettings set org.gnome.nautilus.preferences default-sort-order 'type'
gsettings set org.gnome.nautilus.preferences default-sort-in-reverse-order false

# Enable folders-first sorting in GTK 3 and GTK 4 FileChooser schemas
gsettings set org.gtk.Settings.FileChooser sort-directories-first true
gsettings set org.gtk.gtk4.Settings.FileChooser sort-directories-first true

If a GTK schema is not exposed directly to gsettings in your current session, write the underlying keys using dconf:

dconf write /org/gtk/settings/file-chooser/sort-directories-first true
dconf write /org/gtk/gtk4/settings/file-chooser/sort-directories-first true

Applying Changes Globally

Restart Nautilus and clear cached per-folder GVfs metadata so the new defaults apply recursively across all directories:

nautilus -q
rm -rf ~/.local/share/gvfs-metadata

Power Management, Battery Thresholds, and Lid Switch Policies

Power behavior on modern Fedora GNOME systems spans three subsystems: gsettings for idle sleep timeouts, UPower over D-Bus (busctl) for battery charge thresholds, and systemd-logind for physical lid-switch events.

Idle Sleep and Suspend Timeouts (gsettings)

Control inactive sleep timeouts and automatic suspend actions via org.gnome.settings-daemon.plugins.power:

# Inspect current sleep and suspend settings
gsettings list-recursively org.gnome.settings-daemon.plugins.power | grep sleep

# Set sleep timeout on battery (in seconds, e.g., 900 = 15 minutes)
gsettings set org.gnome.settings-daemon.plugins.power sleep-inactive-battery-timeout 900

# Disable automatic suspend on AC power and battery
gsettings set org.gnome.settings-daemon.plugins.power sleep-inactive-ac-type 'nothing'
gsettings set org.gnome.settings-daemon.plugins.power sleep-inactive-battery-type 'nothing'

To prevent the GDM login screen from suspending automatically while idle:

sudo -u gdm dbus-run-session gsettings set org.gnome.settings-daemon.plugins.power sleep-inactive-ac-type 'nothing'

Battery Charging Thresholds (busctl / UPower)

Note

GNOME's native Preserve Battery Health vs. Maximize Charge option does not use a gsettings key; instead, it communicates directly with UPower over D-Bus.

First, locate your battery's UPower device path and inspect its supported methods:

upower -e | grep battery
busctl introspect org.freedesktop.UPower /org/freedesktop/UPower/devices/battery_BAT0

Toggle the charge threshold (replace battery_BAT0 if your system uses a different battery identifier):

# Enable "Preserve Battery Health" (caps charge around 80%)
busctl call org.freedesktop.UPower /org/freedesktop/UPower/devices/battery_BAT0 org.freedesktop.UPower.Device EnableChargeThreshold b true

# Set to "Maximize Charge" (allows charging to 100%)
busctl call org.freedesktop.UPower /org/freedesktop/UPower/devices/battery_BAT0 org.freedesktop.UPower.Device EnableChargeThreshold b false

Preventing Sleep on Laptop Lid Close (systemd-logind)

Note

Modern GNOME releases removed lid-close action keys from gsettings (such as lid-close-ac-action) and delegate hardware lid-switch handling directly to systemd-logind.

To permanently ignore lid-close events across battery, AC power, and docked states, create a drop-in configuration file for systemd-logind:

sudo mkdir -p /etc/systemd/logind.conf.d
sudo tee /etc/systemd/logind.conf.d/lid.conf << 'EOF'
[Login]
HandleLidSwitch=ignore
HandleLidSwitchExternalPower=ignore
HandleLidSwitchDocked=ignore
EOF

Restart systemd-logind to apply the policy immediately (note that restarting systemd-logind may terminate your active graphical session):

sudo systemctl restart systemd-logind

If you only want to prevent sleep temporarily while a specific task runs, use systemd-inhibit instead of modifying system configuration files:

systemd-inhibit --what=handle-lid-switch sleep 3600

Finishing Touches

Combining gsettings, dconf, busctl, and systemd-logind gives you complete command-line control over your Fedora GNOME workstation, making it straightforward to version-control and replicate your exact desktop, file manager, and power configuration across fresh installs.

item.title: Syncing Files from macOS to Fedora Linux with rsync and SSH
item.description:
When transferring files between a macOS workstation (such as my MacBook Air ankaa) and a Fedora Linux machine (my Lenovo ThinkPad T450 taylor), rsync over SSH provides fast, incremental synchronization. Once the taylor host alias is configured in ~/.ssh/config, rsync automatically inherits your target IP address (192.168.0.10), username, and custom identity key without requiring explicit connection flags on every run.

The Recommended Command Structure (Short Flags)

The standard pattern for copying files from macOS to a remote Linux host uses compact short options:

rsync -avzP /path/to/local/source/ taylor:/path/to/remote/destination/

Flag Breakdown (-avzP)

  • `-a` (archive mode): Preserves file permissions, ownership, timestamps, and symbolic links recursively.
  • `-v` (verbose): Displays which files are being transferred.
  • `-z` (compress): Compresses data in transit to speed up transfers over Wi-Fi or LAN.
  • `-P` (progress and partial): Displays real-time progress bars and retains partially transferred files to allow resuming interrupted transfers.

Common Use Cases and Trailing Slashes

  1. Transferring a Single File:

    rsync -avzP ~/Downloads/document.pdf taylor:~/Downloads/

  2. Transferring an Entire Folder:

    Pay close attention to the trailing slash (/) on the source directory:

    • Copy the contents of a directory into a target folder (note the trailing slash on Photos/):

      rsync -avzP ~/Photos/ taylor:~/Pictures/

      (Result: Files inside ``~/Photos/`` are placed directly inside ``~/Pictures/`` on ``taylor``).

    • Copy the directory itself as a subdirectory (no trailing slash on Photos):

      rsync -avzP ~/Photos taylor:~/Pictures/

      (Result: Creates ``~/Pictures/Photos/`` on ``taylor``).

Safe Verification: Run a Dry Run First (-n)

To preview which files will be copied or updated without modifying anything on disk, pass the -n (or --dry-run) flag:

rsync -avzPn ~/Documents/ taylor:~/Documents/

Once you confirm the file list looks accurate, remove the n flag to perform the live transfer.

Short Flags vs. Long Options

Short options (like -a, -v, -z) are single-letter abbreviations designed for quick terminal input. Long options (like --archive, --verbose, --compress) perform the exact same operations while remaining self-documenting and easier to read in scripts and documentation.

Short Flag Equivalent Long Option What It Does
-a --archive Enables recursion and preserves permissions, modification times, ownership, and symlinks.
-v --verbose Displays detailed information about which files are being transferred.
-z --compress Compresses file data during network transit to speed up transfer times over Wi-Fi.
-P --progress --partial Combined shortcut: --progress shows the live bar; --partial keeps incomplete files if the connection breaks for resuming.
-n --dry-run Performs a trial run showing what would change without transferring or modifying any files.
-u --update Skips files that are already newer on the destination host (taylor).

What --update Adds to Your Workflow

Adding --update instructs rsync to compare file timestamps across both machines:

  • If a file on taylor is newer than the corresponding file on your Mac, rsync will not overwrite it.
  • This prevents accidentally rolling back recent edits made directly on the remote Linux workstation.

Recommended Command Structure (Long Options)

Using explicit long options, the standard transfer syntax becomes:

rsync --archive --verbose --update --compress --progress --partial /path/to/local/source/ taylor:/path/to/remote/destination/

Note

--compress is optional over fast local networks, though still recommended when transferring large text files, source code repositories, or scripts.

Long-Option Use Cases and Dry Runs

  1. Transferring a Single File:

    rsync --archive --verbose --update --progress --partial ~/Downloads/document.pdf taylor:~/Downloads/

  2. Transferring Directory Contents vs. Subdirectories:

    • Copy contents directly (trailing slash on Photos/):

      rsync --archive --verbose --update --compress --progress --partial ~/Photos/ taylor:~/Pictures/

    • Copy the directory itself (no trailing slash on Photos):

      rsync --archive --verbose --update --compress --progress --partial ~/Photos taylor:~/Pictures/

  3. Running a Dry Run with Long Options:

    rsync --dry-run --archive --verbose --update --progress --partial ~/Documents/ taylor:~/Documents/

Filtering macOS Metadata Files

macOS automatically generates hidden metadata files such as .DS_Store and .localized that clutter Linux directories. You can exclude them per command or configure a permanent global exclusion list.

Option 1: Inline Exclusions (Per-Command)

Pass individual --exclude parameters directly to rsync:

rsync --archive --verbose --update --progress --partial \
  --exclude='.DS_Store' \
  --exclude='.localized' \
  --exclude='._*' \
  --exclude='.CFUserTextEncoding' \
  ~/Desktop/ taylor:~/Desktop/

Common macOS metadata files to exclude include:

  • .DS_Store (Finder folder display settings)
  • .localized (system folder localization hints)
  • ._* (AppleDouble resource fork files created on non-HFS/APFS volumes)
  • .CFUserTextEncoding (user text encoding preferences)
  • .Trashes and .Spotlight-V100 (system trash and Spotlight index directories)

One-Liner with Zsh Brace Expansion

Because macOS uses zsh as its default shell, you can collapse multiple --exclude flags into a single brace expansion one-liner:

rsync --archive --verbose --update --progress --partial --exclude={'.DS_Store','.localized','._*','.CFUserTextEncoding'} ~/Desktop/ taylor:~/Desktop/

The shell expands {...} into separate --exclude arguments before executing rsync.

Option 2: Permanent Global Exclusion List (Recommended)

To avoid typing exclusion flags repeatedly, define a global ignore file in your home directory and alias rsync in ~/.zshrc.

  1. Create ``~/.rsync-exclude`` on macOS:

    cat << 'EOF' > ~/.rsync-exclude
.DS_Store
.localized
._*
.CFUserTextEncoding
.Trashes
.Spotlight-V100
EOF

  2. Add an alias to ``~/.zshrc``:

    Open ~/.zshrc in your editor:

    nano ~/.zshrc

    Append the following line and save the file:

    alias rsync='rsync --exclude-from="$HOME/.rsync-exclude"'

    Reload your shell configuration:

    source ~/.zshrc

  3. Run your standard sync command:

    rsync --archive --verbose --update --progress --partial ~/Desktop/ taylor:~/Desktop/

Cleaning Up Existing Metadata Files on Linux

If macOS metadata files were already synced to taylor previously, you can remove them remotely via SSH:

ssh taylor "find ~/Desktop -name '.DS_Store' -o -name '.localized' -delete"

SSH Host Key Troubleshooting and Connection Verification

When reinstalling Fedora Linux on taylor while retaining the same local IP address (192.168.0.10), SSH generates a new host key fingerprint. Attempting to copy keys or connect from ankaa will trigger a remote host identification warning because the stored fingerprint in ~/.ssh/known_hosts no longer matches.

Step 1: Remove the Stale Host Key Entry

Clear the old fingerprint for 192.168.0.10 from ankaa:

ssh-keygen -R 192.168.0.10

This removes the outdated entry from ~/.ssh/known_hosts and saves a backup copy of the previous file.

Step 2: Copy Your Public Key and Accept the New Fingerprint

Re-run ssh-copy-id using your custom-named public key:

ssh-copy-id -i ~/.ssh/porfirio@ankaa.pub porfirio@192.168.0.10

Type yes when prompted to trust the new host fingerprint, then enter your Fedora password to install the public key on taylor.

Step 3: Configure ~/.ssh/config and Test Connections

Ensure your SSH client configuration on ankaa points to the private key file (without the .pub extension):

nano ~/.ssh/config

Host taylor
    HostName 192.168.0.10
    User porfirio
    IdentityFile ~/.ssh/porfirio@ankaa

Enforce strict permissions on the configuration file:

chmod 600 ~/.ssh/config

You can now verify passwordless authentication using three methods:

  1. Direct connection with explicit identity flag:

    ssh -i ~/.ssh/porfirio@ankaa porfirio@192.168.0.10

  2. Non-interactive remote command execution:

    ssh -i ~/.ssh/porfirio@ankaa porfirio@192.168.0.10 "hostname; uptime"

  3. Alias-based connection:

    ssh taylor

If SSH still prompts for a password, run the connection in verbose mode (-v) to inspect key negotiation:

ssh -v -i ~/.ssh/porfirio@ankaa porfirio@192.168.0.10

item.title: Seamless SSH Agent Forwarding and Keychain Management Between macOS and Linux
item.description:
When connecting via SSH from a primary workstation to a remote Linux machine, the remote shell initializes as an isolated environment. By default, it does not inherit your local machine's active ssh-agent session, nor does it automatically spawn a new agent or load custom-named private keys unless explicitly configured to do so.

For example, when I SSH from my MacBook Air (ankaa) into my Lenovo ThinkPad T450 running Fedora Linux (taylor) to work on my Pelican blog repository, running git fetch or git push against GitHub on taylor will fail with Permission denied (publickey) if no active agent socket is available. While running eval "$(ssh-agent -s)" and ssh-add manually on the remote host solves the issue for a single session, OpenSSH provides a much cleaner, permanent workflow via client configuration.

By combining agent forwarding on the client side with native OS credential integration, you can authenticate Git operations and secondary SSH jumps from a remote Linux host without ever copying private keys onto it.

Core SSH Client Directives

To manage SSH key lifecycles automatically on macOS and forward credentials securely to a Linux host, three primary directives in ~/.ssh/config work together:

1. AddKeysToAgent yes

  • What it does: Automatically loads your private SSH key into the running ssh-agent memory the first time you use it.
  • Why it matters: Instead of manually running ssh-add after every system reboot or new terminal session, OpenSSH silently registers the key the moment you initiate a connection.

2. UseKeychain yes

  • What it does: Integrates OpenSSH with native macOS Keychain Services.
  • Why it matters: When you unlock an encrypted SSH key with its passphrase on macOS, the passphrase is stored securely in your Keychain. On subsequent logins or reboots, ssh-agent retrieves the passphrase automatically so you do not have to re-enter it.

Note

UseKeychain is a macOS-specific OpenSSH option. If you share your ~/.ssh/config across Linux systems like taylor, OpenSSH on Linux will ignore it or require IgnoreUnknown UseKeychain at the top of the configuration file.

3. ForwardAgent yes

  • What it does: Passes your local machine's active ssh-agent socket through the encrypted SSH tunnel to the remote host.
  • Why it matters: Remote processes—such as git interacting with GitHub—can request cryptographic signatures directly from your local agent. Your private key never leaves your local machine; only authentication challenges and signatures traverse the encrypted channel.

Warning

Only enable ForwardAgent yes on trusted remote hosts where you control root access, as a privileged user on the remote machine could temporarily access the forwarded socket while your session is active.

Configuring the Client Machine (macOS)

To put this workflow into practice, configure your SSH client on the initiating machine. Using my setup as a working example, I configure ~/.ssh/config on ankaa (macOS) to define connection parameters for taylor (Fedora Linux).

Step 1: Edit ~/.ssh/config

Open your SSH client configuration file on your local machine:

nano ~/.ssh/config

Add a host definition block specifying the target address, user, identity file, and agent directives:

Host taylor
    HostName <taylor-ip-or-hostname>
    User porfirio
    IdentityFile ~/.ssh/id_ed25519
    AddKeysToAgent yes
    UseKeychain yes
    ForwardAgent yes

(Replace ``<taylor-ip-or-hostname>`` and ``porfirio`` with your target host's IP address or local hostname and username).

Step 2: Enforce Strict Configuration Permissions

OpenSSH enforces StrictModes on configuration files as well as keys. Ensure your ~/.ssh/config file is readable and writable only by your user account:

chmod 600 ~/.ssh/config

Verifying the Workflow on the Remote Host

Once the configuration block is saved on ankaa, connecting and authenticating remote Git operations requires zero manual agent management:

  1. Initiate the SSH connection from ankaa:

    ssh taylor

  2. macOS automatically loads ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 into ssh-agent, unlocks it via Keychain, and forwards the agent socket to taylor.

  3. On taylor, verify that the forwarded identity is visible to the remote shell:

    ssh-add -l

  4. Navigate to a repository and run remote Git operations directly against GitHub without storing local keys on taylor:

    cd ~/gitRepos/github.com/porfiriopaiz/site
git fetch origin
git switch devel

Finishing Touches

With AddKeysToAgent, UseKeychain, and ForwardAgent properly configured, your primary workstation acts as a single, secure credential vault. You can seamlessly administer remote Linux systems and interact with authenticated Git repositories while keeping your private keys isolated on a single physical device.

item.title: Installing Cisco Packet Tracer on Fedora 44 Workstation Using Distrobox
item.description:
Cisco Packet Tracer is an essential tool for CCNA students and network engineers. However, Cisco officially distributes Packet Tracer as a .deb package targeting Ubuntu Linux, making native installation on RPM-based distributions like Fedora 44 Workstation tricky.

Rather than dirtying your host Fedora system with converted RPMs or extracted binaries, the cleanest solution is to isolate Cisco Packet Tracer inside an Ubuntu 24.04 Noble Numbat container via Distrobox.

This guide covers all prerequisite packages, container setup, dependency fixes, FUSE symlinks, and desktop integration for Fedora 44 Workstation Edition.

Host Prerequisites (Fedora 44 Workstation)

Before creating the container, ensure your host system has Distrobox, Podman, and the legacy FUSE kernel tools installed.

Open a terminal on your Fedora host (taylor) and install the host prerequisites:

sudo dnf install -y distrobox podman fuse
  • podman / distrobox: Provides the container runtime and seamless host integration.
  • fuse: Enables host-level FUSE mounting capabilities required by AppImage binaries inside containers.

Step 1: Create and Enter the Ubuntu Container

Create an Ubuntu 24.04 container named ubuntu-pt:

distrobox-create --name ubuntu-pt --image ubuntu:24.04

Once creation completes, enter the container shell:

distrobox-enter -n ubuntu-pt

Step 2: Install Container Base Dependencies

Inside your ubuntu-pt container shell, update package lists and install the core desktop and FUSE dependencies required by Ubuntu 24.04:

sudo apt update
sudo apt install -y fuse3 libglib2.0-bin desktop-file-utils shared-mime-info

Setting Up the FUSE Symlink

Cisco Packet Tracer's internal AppImage loader specifically calls fusermount, whereas Ubuntu 24.04 relies on fusermount3. Create a symbolic link inside the container to prevent AppImage mounting failures:

sudo ln -sf /usr/bin/fusermount3 /usr/bin/fusermount

Step 3: Install Cisco Packet Tracer .deb Package

Download the CiscoPacketTracer_901_Ubuntu_64bit.deb file into your host ~/Downloads directory (which is automatically mounted inside Distrobox).

Inside the container, navigate to your downloads folder and install the package:

sudo apt install ./Downloads/CiscoPacketTracer_901_Ubuntu_64bit.deb

Note

You may see a notice stating: N: Download is performed unsandboxed as root.... This is safe to ignore; it simply indicates apt fell back to root privileges to read files from your home directory.

During installation, accept the End User License Agreement (EULA). When prompted:

Would you like to run multi-user when application starts?

Select No unless you are setting up a multi-tenant shared computer lab.

Step 4: Resolve Runtime GUI and Library Dependencies

Cisco Packet Tracer depends on several dynamic libraries that are omitted from minimal container base images. Run the following command inside the container to install all missing audio, graphics, security, and XCB display dependencies:

sudo apt install -y \
    libopengl0 \
    libgl1 \
    libnss3 \
    libnspr4 \
    libxss1 \
    libasound2t64 \
    libpulse0 \
    libxcb-xinerama0 \
    libxcb-cursor0 \
    libxkbcommon-x11-0 \
    libxcb-icccm4 \
    libxcb-image0 \
    libxcb-keysyms1 \
    libxcb-randr0 \
    libxcb-render-util0 \
    libxcb-shape0 \
    libxcb-xfixes0

Summary of key dependencies:

  • libopengl0 & libgl1: Provides OpenGL rendering for the device canvas.
  • libnss3 & libnspr4: Enables internal web view components.
  • libasound2t64 & libpulse0: Handles PulseAudio client audio routing.
  • libxcb-*: Provides X11/XCB platform plugins for Qt application window rendering.

Now exit the container shell:

exit

Step 5: Desktop Integration on Fedora Host

To launch Cisco Packet Tracer directly from your Fedora GNOME Application menu, create a custom .desktop launcher entry on your host system.

Open your text editor on the Fedora host:

vi ~/.local/share/applications/packettracer.desktop

Paste the following configuration:

[Desktop Entry]
Name=Cisco Packet Tracer
Comment=Networking Simulation Tool
Exec=distrobox-enter -n ubuntu-pt -- packettracer
Terminal=false
Type=Application
Categories=Education;Network;
StartupNotify=true

Save the file and update the desktop launcher database:

update-desktop-database ~/.local/share/applications/

Testing the Installation

You can now launch Cisco Packet Tracer directly from your terminal:

distrobox-enter -n ubuntu-pt -- packettracer

Or simply search for Cisco Packet Tracer in your GNOME Super/Activities launcher!

item.title: Installing TeX Live 2025 on Fedora: A Minimalist User-Space Guide
item.description:
This guide consolidates the steps required to establish a professional-grade LaTeX environment into a single, clean workflow. Following this chronological order ensures that directories exist, dependencies are met, and the environment is correctly configured before the software attempts to utilize them.

By installing TeX Live in user-space (within ~/.local/opt), we adhere to a minimalist philosophy. This approach avoids cluttering the system root, removes the need for sudo during package management via tlmgr, and ensures you are using the most recent upstream binaries rather than potentially outdated distribution packages.

Pre-Installation: System Dependencies

Fedora's "minimal" Perl and X11 profiles often lack specific libraries required by the TeX Live installer and its graphical management tools. While we aim for a lean system, these Perl modules are essential for the installer's checksum verification and the tlmgr interface.

Install these requirements using dnf:

sudo dnf install perl-File-Find perl-File-Copy perl-Digest-MD5 perl-Tk perl-Term-ANSIColor xdotool

Create the Directory Structure

We will create a "user-space system" directory. Utilizing ~/.local/opt keeps your home directory organized while mimicking the Linux Filesystem Hierarchy Standard (FHS).

mkdir -p ~/.local/bin

mkdir -p ~/.local/opt/texlive

Download and Launch the Installer

To avoid "checksum mismatch" errors common with unstable local mirrors, we will point the installer directly to the Comprehensive TeX Archive Network (CTAN) global repository.

cd ~/Downloads

wget http://mirror.ctan.org/systems/texlive/tlnet/install-tl-unx.tar.gz

tar -xzf install-tl-unx.tar.gz

cd install-tl-*

Launch the installer using a reliable global mirror:

./install-tl -repository http://mirror.ctan.org/systems/texlive/tlnet/

Installer Configuration (Text Menu)

Once the command-line interface menu appears, you must modify specific installation paths to point to your local directories:

  1. Directories (D): Change TEXDIR to: /home/porfirio/.local/opt/texlive/2025
  2. Options (O): * Toggle Paper Size to letter. * Toggle Create symlinks (L) to [X]. * Binaries: /home/porfirio/.local/bin * Manpages: /home/porfirio/.local/share/man * Info: /home/porfirio/.local/share/info
  3. Install (I): Start the process.

Note

The full installation can take approximately 3 hours depending on your connection. It is highly recommended to run this inside a tmux session to prevent the installation from terminating if your terminal session disconnects.

Post-Installation: Environment Setup

Fedora needs to be instructed where to find these new binaries. We will create a modular profile script in ~/.bashrc.d/ to keep our ~/.bashrc clean.

Create the configuration file:

vi ~/.bashrc.d/texlive.sh

Paste the following content into the file:

# TeX Live 2025 Path Configuration
TEX_BIN_PATH="/home/porfirio/.local/opt/texlive/2025/bin/x86_64-linux"

if [ -d "$TEX_BIN_PATH" ]; then
    # Prioritize TeX binaries and your local bin folder
    export PATH="$TEX_BIN_PATH:/home/porfirio/.local/bin:$PATH"
    export INFOPATH="/home/porfirio/.local/opt/texlive/2025/texmf-dist/doc/info:$INFOPATH"
    export MANPATH="/home/porfirio/.local/opt/texlive/2025/texmf-dist/doc/man:$MANPATH"
fi

Apply the changes to your current session:

source ~/.bashrc

Finalizing the Formats

With the paths set and Perl dependencies satisfied, manually execute the tasks that occasionally fail during the installer's finalization stage due to environment restrictions:

# Set default paper size
tlmgr paper letter

# Build the format files (Engines)
fmtutil-sys --all

Verification and Troubleshooting

To ensure your system is ready for document production, perform a "smoke test" by checking the binary location and compiling a dummy document.

Check the Binary Path

which pdflatex

This should return a path pointing to your ~/.local/bin/ or ~/.local/opt/ folder rather than /usr/bin/.

Compile a Test Document

echo "\documentclass{article}\begin{document}LaTeX 2025 is Live on Fedora!\end{document}" > test.tex

pdflatex test.tex

Summary of Locations

For future maintenance on your system, keep these paths in mind:

  • The System Root: ~/.local/opt/texlive/2025/
  • The Binaries/Symlinks: ~/.local/bin/
  • The Configuration: ~/.bashrc.d/texlive.sh
  • The Logs: ~/.local/opt/texlive/2025/texmf-var/web2c/fmtutil.log

You now have a professional-grade, upstream LaTeX installation that is completely independent of Fedora's system packages, making it easy to back up or migrate to a new machine in the future.
